issue_context.title: Bevy crashes when not found any audio device
issue_context.body:
**Bevy version**


**Operating system & version**
Ubuntu 20.10 docker

**What you did**

I wanted to run bevy inside ubuntu docker image 

**What you expected to happen**

App should open properly

**What actually happened**
This error was shown and later crash happens
```
ALSA lib confmisc.c:767:(parse_card) cannot find card '0'
ALSA lib conf.c:4743:(_snd_config_evaluate) function snd_func_card_driver returned error: No such file or directory
ALSA lib confmisc.c:392:(snd_func_concat) error evaluating strings
ALSA lib conf.c:4743:(_snd_config_evaluate) function snd_func_concat returned error: No such file or directory
ALSA lib confmisc.c:1246:(snd_func_refer) error evaluating name
ALSA lib conf.c:4743:(_snd_config_evaluate) function snd_func_refer returned error: No such file or directory
ALSA lib conf.c:5231:(snd_config_expand) Evaluate error: No such file or directory
ALSA lib pcm.c:2660:(snd_pcm_open_noupdate) Unknown PCM default
thread 'main' panicked at 'The device doesn't support any format!?: DeviceNotAvailable', /root/.cargo/registry/src/github.com-1ecc6299db9ec823/rodio-0.13.0/src/stream.rs:191:30
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```

**Additional information**
When not found audio device, bevy shouldn't crash but only show error - https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio/issues/334

**Steps to reproduce**
- Open 20.10 docker image
- Install xvfb `apt install xvfb`
- Download and compile Mesa from source and install it  (it contains LavaPipe, which allow to run Vulkan app in CI)
- Clone Bevy
- `cargo run --example clear_color` (it is a little strange that this example needs audio)
- `xvfb-run target/debug/examples/clear_color`

I work out a solution for **ubuntu container** (20.04) without audio device:

1. Inside container, Install audio package by: `apt install -y pulseaudio`
2. Set audio source as described in [here](https://superuser.com/a/1545361), to be specific:
    1. Give audio access to current user: `adduser $(id -u -n) pulse-access`
    2. `rm -rf /var/run/pulse /var/lib/pulse /root/.config/pulse`
    3. `pulseaudio -D --verbose --exit-idle-time=-1 --system --disallow-exit`
3. Run your problem: `cargo run`

I have noticed this same issue on many different machines. I don't think this is as much a driver issue as it is a problem that should be addressed with Bevy. Bevy should opt out of audio before crashing, or at least, it should allow the developer to make this decision. Many applications and even games are fine without audio and a developer shouldn't have to offer two versions of a program (one with and one without audio dependencies).

I know there has been discussion to change the audio system in Bevy, perhaps this should be addressed there? @Moxinilian @Dash-L

Yeah I agree that Bevy shouldn't crash in this case. Ideally it just displays an error message when a device can't be found (and probably when audio is played but no device is available). Additionally, it would be great if it could gracefully respond to devices being connected / defaults being switched.

This issue is present in Windows as well, although the error message is different.

```
thread 'main' panicked at 'called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: NoDevice', C:\Users\forbjok\.cargo\registry\src\github.com-1ecc6299db9ec823\bevy_audio-0.5.0\src\audio_output.rs:22:67
```

While it's probably not super common to not have an audio device, it definitely should not cause a crash.

review_comments:
If you try to `play_source` when there is no audio device, I don't like the behavior of silentely succeeding. 
I would expect this to either
1) `error!`
2) `panic!`
3) have this return like `Result<(), ()>` (or some other error type)

From the player point of view, an `error` or `panic` are bad. "ok I know I don't have a audio device, don't crash and don't yell at me!". There's already a `warn` on the creation, re-logging it every time a sound play doesn't add much...

That's fair. However, I have the counter argument that if you don't have an audio device, and therefore the `stream_handle` is `None`, if you are trying to play an `audio_source`, that's incorrect. Calling these functions if the type itself is not constructed successfully and then "working" seems a little off. 😅 It's fine if you try to create the `AudioSource` and that fails, (and it doesn't panic) however, if you actually try to play audio with that audio source, that probably shouldn't work. Ultimately I'm fine with this PR as is though. I think it's just important to consider how silently succeeding can be harmful. :smiley: Arguable, we should remove the `default` implementation, and instead do something like: ```rust impl

AudioOutput

{ pub fn new() -> Option; } ``` However, I don't think this is actually possible, since it needs `Default` to be initialized as a resource.

While `init_resource` requires `default` (actually `FromWorld`, but that has a blanket implementation for types that implement `default`), `insert_resource` doesn't have that bound.

An alternative is that `AudioOutput` is just never inserted as a Resource, and systems need to query for `Option<Res<AudioOutput>>` instead of `Res<AudioOutput>`

> An alternative is that AudioOutput is just never inserted as a Resource, and systems need to query for Option<Res<AudioOutput>> instead of Res<AudioOutput>

Something like this would be my preferred solution :)
I'm temporarily removing the `ready for cart` label until we decide on the best path forward from the above discussion.

> if you don't have an audio device, and therefore the `stream_handle` is `None`, if you are trying to play an `audio_source`, that's incorrect

I disagree with that. The absence of an audio device isn't something I would really consider an error at all, it's just a possible circumstance on a user's computer. I would generally expect that if you run a game on a system that has no audio device, it should behave exactly the same as if you do have an audio device and just muted the volume. No sound, but the game runs perfectly fine otherwise.

Ideally, I would have preferred to be able to be able to disconnect and reconnect audio devices, or change the default output device at runtime and have it "just work" and play newly played sounds through the correct device, but that would likely require a bigger change. Currently, if you disconnect the only audio device while Bevy is running, the audio will just stop working and no more audio will be played even if you plug it back in, unless you restart the game.

> The absence of an audio device isn't something I would really consider an error at all, it's just a possible circumstance on a user's computer

I don't disagree with this. :)
What I was saying is that if you don't have an audio device (which is ok) then the `AudioOutput` should not succeed in creation. And since the output didn't succeed you shouldn't be able to call `play_source` since the output doesn't exist. 

If we want to support not panicking when a device (`AudioOutput`) isn't available, that should be at the system level (as @MinerSebas recommended).

From my pov, it just seems like we're trying to shove the logic of error handling inside the `AudioOutput` where I would prefer it to be handled at a different level (e.g. the system level)

However, if people really prefer the current implementation, I'm more than happy to mark this as resolved 🙂

> An alternative is that `AudioOutput` is just never inserted as a Resource, and systems need to query for `Option<Res<AudioOutput>>` instead of `Res<AudioOutput>`

The issue with this is that it would require users of Bevy to have an `if let Some(audio_output) = audio output` in every place where audio is being played. This seems very inelegant and clunky. I think it's much better to have AudioOutput itself always exist, and have it handle the existence (or non-existence) of devices internally so that users don't have to worry about it.

I experimented a bit with changing it so that the streams are stored in a RefCell (initialized to None by default) and then initialized on demand, and while this basically works and solves the problem of Bevy crashing, I wasn't able to find a way to detect when the stored OutputStreamHandle has broken due to the device having been disconnected, so being able to recover from that might require changes in `rodio`.

UPDATE: Pushed the RefCell experiment to branch `fix-no-audio-device-crash2` on my Bevy repository. Did not push it to the pull request branch, as it currently has no functional benefit over the original change.

>  I think it's much better to have AudioOutput itself always exist, and have it handle the existence

Sure, and when you phrase it like that I don't mind it as much :)
Feel free to marked the thread as resolved and thanks for the discussion 👍

> The issue with this is that it would require users of Bevy to have an `if let Some(audio_output) = audio` output in every place where audio is being played. This seems very inelegant and clunky. 

Using `if let` is a *very* common pattern in Rust. Unlike most other languages, Rust has a *very* strong priority on correctness, it really pushes you to manually handle failure conditions rather than silently ignoring them.

Rust was never designed as a loose scripting language where you can just do whatever and have it "just work", and trying to make it into a loose scripting language will have a lot of long term negative effects.

I can also see plenty of situations where it is *mandatory* to have audio, or where the programmer wants to handle audio failure in a specific way. Using `Option` to represent a missing resource or component is correct.

> The absence of an audio device isn't something I would really consider an error at all, it's just a possible circumstance on a user's computer

That is correct, it is not an error, but it *is* a *failure*. Rust makes a clear distinction between failures and errors. If a key is missing in a dictionary, that is a failure (which is why [`HashMap::get`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.HashMap.html#method.get) returns an `Option`). Rust has very good systems for handling failures (`if let`, `match`, `?`, `try`, and combinators).

Other languages also have a distinction between [errors and failures](https://www.joyent.com/node-js/production/design/errors), but this distinction is implicit (not explicit), and many programmers are unaware of the distinction. In Rust the distinction is explicit (`Option` vs `Result` vs panic).

> I can also see plenty of situations where it is _mandatory_ to have audio, or where the programmer wants to handle audio failure in a specific way.

For these most likely extremely rare cases, I think it would make more sense to have a way to explicitly check whether an audio device is present.

> That is correct, it is not an error, but it _is_ a _failure_. Rust makes a clear distinction between failures and errors.

This argument makes sense in the context of a low-level audio library, but not so much in the context of a game engine.

I would argue that from the perspective of a user of the engine (game developer), as well as end-users, trying to play a sound when there is no audio device connected is not even a failure. For all intents and purposes, it's the same as if you play audio through a sound device that is muted or doesn't have a speaker plugged in. You obviously don't get any sound, but it is not in any way wrong of the game to try to play sound.

> For these most likely extremely rare cases, I think it would make more sense to have a way to explicitly check whether an audio device is present.

Yes, that is exactly what `Option` is. And the case is not "extreme", it is quite common for games to inform the user about missing hardware.

> This argument makes sense in the context of a low-level audio library, but not so much in the context of a game engine.

Not at all, the distinction is pervasive at all levels, it has nothing to do with "low level" vs "high level". Every language (including high level scripting languages like JavaScript) has this concept. The link in my previous comment explains this in more detail. It is simply a fundamental programming principle.

> I would argue that from the perspective of a user of the engine (game developer), as well as end-users, trying to play a sound when there is no audio device connected is not even a failure.

In some cases that may be true, but in some cases it is not. That's why it should be `Option`, so the programmer can *choose* what behavior they want:

* They can ignore the failure.
* They can propagate the failure to somewhere else.
* They can retry again later.
* They can crash.
* They can report the failure in some way.
* Some combination of the above.

Using `Option` gives complete control to the programmer.

> For all intents and purposes, it's the same as if you play audio through a sound device that is muted or doesn't have a speaker plugged in.

That's not true. If the audio is muted that is an explicit choice by the user. If the audio is failing, that is generally *not* the user's choice, instead it is caused by some sort of bug, hardware failure, or misconfiguration.

The game might wish to display a popup box to the user saying "Could not find audio device, make sure your audio is configured properly". If the game does *not* inform the user of the problem, then the user will wonder, "why is my audio not working?"

> You obviously don't get any sound, but it is not in any way wrong of the game to try to play sound.

As I said, you must distinguish between failure and errors. It is not *wrong* for a dictionary to be missing a key, but it is a failure. A failure does not mean something went wrong, it simply means that the operation could not be completed. There is no judgement about "right" or "wrong", because it is not an error.

Just wondering, and very much out of topic, sorry about that... I pretty much always play with no sound because of reasons. Should the volume being off be detected as a failure then?

> Should the volume being off be detected as a failure then?

There's two basic designs:

1. Treat it as not a failure, and have a separate `is_muted` method.
2. Return a `Result` which has an `enum` that describes the various failures that can happen, with `Muted` being one of the reasons.

Either design is fine, they just make different tradeoffs. Personally I would go with the first one.

I agree with the idea that users shouldn't need to care about this (most of the time). I personally don't think the spirit of rust is "whenever you have a chance to require explicit error handling ... do it". I think in rust, just like every other language, you should make a pragmatic call based on the context.

Ex: we _could_ make everyone explicitly handle the case where they try to spawn a sprite, but a render device isn't present by making `spawn().insert(Sprite)` return a RenderDeviceNotAvailable error. But I would argue that doing that would "get in the way" more often than not. A missing render device is a corner case. If every api involving "rendering things" required checking for render device existence, users would have a "very bad time". And when its not there, its generally because the user intended it to be that way (ex; they are running in a headless environment). This is why we have a "headless render backend". We handle this "internally" so when someone tries using sprites, they don't need to think about render devices / account for them being missing.

I would hazard a guess that in the 99.X% case, when users play an audio clip, they don't want to care about audio device existence via `if let` / `unwrap`. Therefore we should have an api that optimizes for that use case. We _should_ still expose "device existence information" to users that care about it. But we constantly make choices to hide information / assume a certain "happy path" state on behalf of our users in the interest of ergonomics and a "pleasant programming experience". This feels like a case where we should do that.

I'm happy to continue this discussion, but I think the current impl is a solid short term solution to a nasty problem. And it has the benefit of not degrading UX for a common use case (and requiring `if let Some(audio_device)` for all audio operation definitely degrades UX for a common use case).
